FIFA said it had been the victim of a criminal cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information, although no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed, according to media reports.
FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information,” a FIFA spokesperson told Al Jazeera.

FIFA strongly condemned the “unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” adding that such actions were “a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy”.
It also said that :”FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.”
FIFA did not say how many people or organisations were affected, when the attack took place or what the business information included. Its reference to publication did not say whether any data had appeared online, or where.
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.

A handout screen grab from an undated video shows Houthi fighters standing on a damaged truck during an offensive against Saudi-backed Yemeni forces in Taiz province [File: EPA]By Sunniya Ahmad PirzadaPublished On 26 Nov 202626 Nov 2026
London, United Kingdom – The United Kingdom has slapped sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis and four of their senior leaders after accusing the Iran-backed group of renewed “aggression” inside Yemen and attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting the financial district in Riyadh this week, as they engage in a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Fighting has escalated since July as a 2022 United Nations-brokered ceasefire collapsed. Since then, the Houthis have captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and the island of Mayyun, extending control over the Red Sea in a setback to the Saudi-backed government.
The war erupted after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, in late 2014, forcing President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the Hadi government as it saw the Iran-backed group’s rise in neighbouring Yemen as a security threat.

LeBron James became the oldest player in NBA history to produce a triple-double, leading Philadelphia to a 114-104 victory over the Miami Heat in the NBA Cup on Wednesday.
Four-time NBA Most Valuable Player James, who turns 42 on December 30, scored a season-high 25 points, passed off a season-high 12 assists and pulled down 10 rebounds to break his own triple-double age mark.

“We wanted to get back to our defensive identity,” James said. “We didn’t do that in the first quarter, but for the next 36 minutes I thought we got back to that.”
The 76ers improved the best record in the Eastern Conference to 15-4 while snapping a seven-game win streak for Miami (10-7).
Both clubs are 2-1 atop Cup East Group B, but with a win, Miami would have clinched the group and advanced to the knockout stage of the in-season tournament.

A view of the oil refinery in Erbil, Iraq [File: Sedat Suna/Getty Images]By AnadoluPublished On 26 Nov 202626 Nov 2026
Iraq’s government has denied local media reports that army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region, as a top court backed Baghdad’s authority over the region’s border crossings and oil in a deepening dispute with Erbil.
Government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi told state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday that there was “no truth” to the media reports. He said oil smugglers were diverting “tens of billions” into “private pockets and accounts”, and that the salaries of Kurdistan’s public employees were not part of the dispute.

Al-Zaidi has ordered the Border Ports Authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdistan region and to close unofficial crossings. He has also ordered federal authorities to take over oil fields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala that are under Kurdish security control.
Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court has issued an interpretive ruling affirming federal powers to secure international borders and deploy armed forces across all Iraqi territory. It also affirmed Baghdad’s right to oversee border crossings, including those in Kurdistan, the production and export of oil and gas, and both oil and non-oil revenues.

An explosion rocked a highway in Cairo when a fuel truck overturned and caught fire, killing at least 31 people on Wednesday.
Egypt’s public prosecutor has announced an investigation into the crash, and the Ministry of Health said it will continue to monitor the situation.

But Egypt is no stranger to deadly accidents on its roads, despite spending billions of dollars on its transportation systems.
So what exactly caused the explosion and how unsafe are Egypt’s roads?
Here is what we know.
What happened?
On Wednesday evening, a fuel tanker travelling on a busy ring road in Giza’s Imbabah district, a highly populated, working-class part of the Greater Cairo area, crashed and exploded, causing a fire that killed at least 31 people and injured 21 others.
Local media have reported that the explosion happened after the truck driver swerved to avoid a high-voltage cable which fell in front of the vehicle.
Twenty-seven vehicles were caught up and burned in the accident, according to Egypt’s judicial office.
Thirty-nine ambulances were dispatched to the scene, taking the injured to nearby hospitals for treatment, the Health Ministry said.

London, United Kingdom – The Jewish Network for Palestine (JNP) has filed an application to reverse the proscription of Hamas under Britain’s Terrorism Act, arguing that the ban is being used against its members and is hampering freedom of speech in the United Kingdom.
The JNP filed a formal de-proscription application on Thursday under Section 4 of the Terrorism Act, which oversees applications to remove a group from the UK’s list of banned organisations.

United States President Donald Trump’s administration has proposed a new slate of trade tariffs against 14 of the US’s key trading partners, including China, India and the European Union.
The tariffs, which would go into effect next year, will hit China the hardest, potentially subjecting its products to a 40 percent import tax.

Washington says the tariffs, announced by the US Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday, are a response to unfair trading practices which harm US manufacturing, including “excess industrial capacity” – subsidies and policies that enable manufacturers to overproduce and undercut the US.
But Trump has long used tariffs as leverage in trade negotiations.
So, is the latest tariff announcement an effort to win concessions in upcoming trade deals? Here’s what we know:
Which economies do the tariffs target, and when would they start?
The tariffs would be imposed on products from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to the USTR. The maximum rates facing each country range from 20 percent to 40 percent.
